content:
The question came from a reporter who had learned nothing from experience.

We were leaving the opening ceremony for the rebuilt eastern bridge when she pushed through the crowd and shouted, “Avatar Aang! Which of your partners will bear the future Air Nation?”

The world stopped.

Not literally.

If it had, Toph would have found a way to blame Aang.

But inside me, something froze.

Aang turned.

Katara’s face went cold.

Toph’s foot struck the stone once.

The reporter, apparently committed to her own destruction, continued.

“Is there an agreement about succession? The public has a legitimate interest in—”

“No,” Aang said.

One word.

Not loud.

Absolute.

The reporter blinked.

Aang stepped toward her.

“The public has no legitimate interest in anyone’s reproductive choices.”

Cameras did not exist in our world, thank the spirits, but I could feel every sketch artist in the crowd committing the moment to history.

The reporter tried again.

“As the last Air Nomad—”

“I am the last surviving Air Nomad,” Aang said. “I am not the owner of every future Air Nomad.”

Katara touched his arm.

Not to stop him.

To stand there.

The reporter looked toward her.

“Master Katara, surely you have discussed—”

Katara smiled.

It was the smile that had destroyed Wen Haru in a hearing room.

“We have discussed boundaries.”

The reporter swallowed.

Toph leaned toward me.

“I can bury her shoes.”

“No.”

“Just the shoes.”

“No.”

Aang ended the questions and we left.

The carriage ride home was silent.

The public statement would be easy.

We had already made the principle clear after the donor meeting.

The private conversation was not easy.

Because the reporter had dragged a question into the open that we had intentionally left unfinished.

Children.

Not Air Nation duty.

Ours.

At home, nobody went to separate rooms.

We ended up at the kitchen table.

Of course.

Toph poured tea badly on purpose and shoved cups toward everyone.

Katara wrapped both hands around hers.

Aang stared at the steam.

I said, “We don’t have to talk about it because somebody else asked.”

Aang looked up.

“Do you want to talk about it?”

I hated the answer.

“Yes.”

Toph groaned. “Fine. But nobody makes a chart.”

I slowly put down my pen.

“Oppression.”

Katara almost laughed.

Aang took a breath.

“I want children someday.”

We knew that.

Hearing it inside this conversation made it new.

He continued. “I don’t know how many. I don’t know what that family looks like. I don’t need biological children from any specific person.”

Toph said, “Good opening.”

Aang gave her a look.

Katara spoke next.

“I think I want children.”

Aang turned toward her.

Katara held up one hand.

“Don’t.”

He stopped.

“I said think.”

His face softened.

“Okay.”

Katara looked down at her tea.

“When I was younger, I assumed I would. Everyone did. Then the war ended and people started talking about Aang’s future children like they already existed.”

Her jaw tightened.

“I hated it enough that sometimes I couldn’t tell whether I didn’t want children or just didn’t want strangers wanting them for me.”

Aang’s face hurt to look at.

He did not interrupt.

Toph tapped one finger against the table.

“My turn?”

Katara nodded.

Toph leaned back.

“I don’t know.”

Simple.

“Kids are loud. Pregnancy sounds horrifying. People already treat my body like public property whenever I’m injured, so that part sounds worse.”

No one corrected the assumption embedded in her specific fear. It was hers to name.

Toph continued. “I like teaching. I like some kids. I don’t want anybody hearing that and deciding it means I secretly want to be a mother.”

“Understood,” I said.

She pointed at me. “Your turn, Paperwork.”

My pulse jumped.

The part of me that resisted fixed answers wanted to dodge the question.

The person living this life needed one honest enough for now.

“I don’t know either.”

Nobody moved.

“I know I don’t want my body treated as an answer to Aang’s culture.”

Aang’s hand tightened around his cup.

“I know.”

This time he caught himself.

“I understand.”

I smiled faintly.

“I know I could love a child. That’s not the same as wanting to raise one.”

Katara nodded.

“I know family can happen in more ways than birth.”

Aang looked at me.

“Adoption?”

“Maybe. Fostering. Nieces and nephews who live in our kitchen. Students who become family. Children one of us has. Children none of us has.”

Toph said, “A very loud collection of strays.”

“You say that like we aren’t already one.”

She grinned.

The pressure eased slightly.

Then Katara asked the hardest question.

“What if one of us wants children and somebody else never does?”

Silence.

There was no answer that turned love into compatibility by force.

Aang stared at the table.

“We would have to decide what that means.”

Toph frowned.

“That’s terrible.”

“Yes.”

“You’re supposed to have a wise Avatar answer.”

“I don’t.”

“Get one.”

Aang laughed once.

Then his expression turned serious again.

“I don’t want staying together to require anybody to become a parent.”

Katara nodded.

“Neither do I.”

Toph said, “Obviously.”

I looked at the three of them.

“And I don’t want staying together to require somebody to give up being a parent if that becomes something they truly need.”

That hurt too.

Because it made room for futures where love was not enough to keep every shape intact.

We sat with it.

No promises we could not know how to keep.

Aang reached across the table.

“Can we agree on now?”

“What about now?” Katara asked.

“No children now.”

Toph raised her hand immediately. “Strong support.”

Katara laughed.

I nodded.

Aang did too.

“Then we revisit it,” he said. “Not because the public asks. Because we do.”

“Yearly?” I asked.

Toph pointed at me. “Chart behavior.”

“Seasonally?”

“Worse.”

Katara said, “When it feels necessary.”

Toph nodded. “Human answer.”

I sighed dramatically and put the pen away.

That night, the newspaper printed the reporter’s question in enormous type.

The answer was smaller.

That seemed typical.

I folded the paper and used it to line the bottom of a kitchen bin.

Aang watched me.

“Symbolic?”

“Practical.”

Toph called from the other room, “Same thing if you do it right!”

I smiled.

The future remained unwritten.

That was not a failure of planning.

No one was owed certainty about our children.

Not donors.

Not reporters.

Not history.

Not even the versions of ourselves sitting around the table tonight.

We owed one another honesty as the answer changed.

Nothing more could be promised without turning possibility into duty.

The reporter’s question followed us home even after we refused to answer it.

Not because it deserved space. Because it had found an existing bruise.

Aang sat at the kitchen table turning his cup between both hands.

“I hate that people think rebuilding the Air Nation means producing airbenders.”

Katara’s expression tightened. “Some people are going to keep thinking it.”

“I know.”

Toph leaned back in her chair. “Then let them be wrong.”

Aang looked toward her.

“They don’t get a vote in our bed,” she added.

Katara choked on her tea.

I laughed hard enough to hurt.

Toph looked pleased with herself.

When the room settled, I said, “I need something clear.”

Three faces turned toward me.

“I can love you and never become part of a plan to restore a people through my body.”

Aang’s face changed instantly—not anger. Pain.

“Yes,” he said.

I held up a hand. “Let me finish.”

He nodded.

“If I ever choose children, that choice cannot become proof of devotion to you. And if I never choose them, that cannot mean I failed you or your culture.”

Aang’s eyes shone.

“Yes.”

This time I let him answer.

Katara reached across the table and took my hand. “Same for me.”

Toph’s voice went flat with certainty. “Obviously.”

Aang exhaled shakily.

“I want Air Nomad culture to live,” he said. “I want airbenders in the world again. I also don’t want any of you turned into… into a duty with a face.”

The words were clumsy.

They were enough because they were his.

We did not solve the future.

We removed one demand from it.

A week later, Aang addressed the question publicly without mentioning any of our private choices.

He spoke about culture, teaching, community, recovered history, and the fact that a people could not be reduced to bloodline arithmetic.

He did not promise future children.

He did not volunteer any of us as evidence.

When he came home, Toph said, “Not terrible.”

Katara kissed him.

I handed him tea.

He looked more relieved by our ordinary reactions than he had by the applause outside.

Afterward, Aang asked whether his answer had been enough.

“It was yours,” I said. “And it left ours private.”

Katara nodded.

Toph added, “Also you didn’t say anything stupid about destiny.”

Aang looked wounded. “I like destiny.”

“We know,” three of us said.

The future felt lighter once nobody had to earn it with a body.

Nobody at our table disagreed.

For that night, that answer was enough.
